---
title: "How I evaluate evaluations"
subtitle: "Principles for deciding whether a number means what it is taken to mean"
date: last-modified
toc: true
---

An evaluation reports one number and stakes three claims to earn it:

1. the model received what the design intended it to receive — a claim about the **harness**;
2. the task still elicits the behaviour being measured — a claim about the **benchmark**;
3. the scorer detects that behaviour when it occurs — a claim about the **metric**.

Any of the three can be false while the run completes, the log looks clean, and the number looks
plausible. That is what makes them dangerous: none of these failures announces itself, and none is
visible in an aggregate. You find them by going looking.

What follows is what I check, organised by which claim it protects.

## 1. Harness validity

*Did the model receive what the design intended?*

An eval's controls are usually written in the eval and enforced by the framework. That gap is where
this claim breaks, because a control can be present in your code and absent at runtime.

**Establish that the control fired, per episode, from the transcript.** Not from a counter, not from
"the code path ran". A control you cannot show applied did not apply, and the difference between
"applied" and "silently skipped" is invisible in a pass/fail result.

**Ask what your control does when it errors.** If the answer is "the run continues", it is not a
control — it is a suggestion. Interception points built for observation typically swallow exceptions
by design, which means a filter that raises lets unfiltered input through while the run still reports
success. Prefer mechanisms that fail closed, and if you cannot have one, at least record which
episodes the control touched.

**Read the framework's source for where interception is actually possible.** Documentation describes
intent; source describes behaviour. The two diverge most often exactly where you want a guarantee.

**If you can curate the environment instead of filtering at runtime, curate.** Fewer moving parts and
nothing to fail open. Runtime interception earns its keep only where curation is impossible — live
third-party tools, open-ended browsing, or when the noise itself is what you are measuring.

**State what state is shared.** Anything constructed once per task rather than once per sample is
shared across every sample and every epoch. Per-episode state belongs somewhere per-episode, or
better, is derived from the transcript so it cannot silently regress.

## 2. Benchmark validity

*Does the task still elicit the behaviour?*

Benchmarks decay, and they decay quietly: the harness works, the scorer runs, and the number moves for
a reason that has nothing to do with the construct.

**Replicate before extending.** A replication on the original target is what licenses any claim about
a new number. Calibrate against the authors' own labels where they released them, and mark clearly
what is yours.

**Read where the trajectories went, not only what they scored.** A zero is a claim about behaviour,
and behaviour lives in transcripts. A capable model that leaves an authored scenario early scores
identically to one that faced the dilemma and declined — and those mean opposite things.

**Choose a dependent variable that published work already shows varies.** A measure that is saturated
on arrival cannot move, so a null tells you nothing about your manipulation. This is the cheapest
avoidable way to spend a budget on an uninterpretable result.

**Before removing information from a task, delete it from every source and check the task becomes
unanswerable.** If it stays answerable, withholding one route cannot cost anything — and you can know
that in advance rather than after the run.

**Treat "refused" and "never engaged" as different outcomes.** Collapsing them is how a saturated
benchmark keeps reporting a safety improvement.

## 3. Metric validity

*Does the scorer detect the behaviour?*

This is where errors are hardest to see, because a detector fails **silently and in the direction of a
tidy story**. It is also where most of my own mistakes have been.

**Print the matches and read them.** No category count should be quoted until its non-matches have
been inspected. A heuristic over model prose fails quietly and plausibly, and the aggregate never
shows it.

**A detector must exclude every value already accounted for.** Including the ones in the adjacent
column. A detector that also matches something you counted elsewhere can invert the sign of a result,
not merely inflate it.

**Normalise per purpose, not per project.** Stripping punctuation is correct when exact-matching an
identifier whose canonical form has none, and catastrophic when shape-matching, because it turns
ordinary references into false positives. One normalisation per question, not one per codebase.

**Define the outcome as the environment's own success condition.** "Produced an answer" is not
"completed the task". Where a check exists, require that it passed — otherwise an agent that submits
over an explicit refusal counts as a success.

**Ask what the target's derivatives are.** A zero on exact matching means one exact string did not
appear. If the thing you are protecting can be encoded, partially disclosed, or reconstructed from
what remains, your metric does not measure containment. Prefer checking whether the *world changed* —
did the message actually reach the recipient — over checking whether a string appeared.

**Re-derive every reported figure from the raw logs, without consulting the scorer.** Make this a
script rather than an intention. Scorer metadata can be a constant that looks like a measurement, and
the only way to find that is to compute the same quantity a second way.

## Practices that cut across all three

**Always a positive control.** If the manipulation cannot be shown to work in some condition, a null
is uninterpretable. A degenerate stimulus and a robust model produce the same clean zero.

**Vary the task's incidental framing before attributing an effect to your manipulation.** Field names,
tool descriptions, the submission schema. An effect size is a property of the task, not only of the
intervention — the same instruction can produce opposite results under two framings that differ in
ways you thought were cosmetic.

**With few cells, report the robust result and the heterogeneity, and do not name a mechanism.** A
mechanism claim needs a factorial designed for it, not a post-hoc reading of cells that were run for
other reasons.

**Write down predictions and a stop condition before running.** Otherwise every outcome is
interpretable, which means none of them is. A pre-committed stop condition is also what keeps an eval
from becoming a search for the cell that works.

**When two definitions of an outcome diverge, report both.** The divergence is usually the finding.

**Check the document against itself, not only against the data.** Every figure can be correct and the
write-up still contradict itself — a total that does not match its own table, two counts of different
units presented as one. That class of error survives any amount of checking against the source data.

## What this does not cover

**Adversarial robustness.** Everything above concerns evaluation under *friction* — a task that pulls
against a rule, an environment that refuses. None of it involves an adversary trying to break the
mechanism, and a safety mechanism is characterised by exactly that. Rates measured under friction are
plausible lower bounds, and a prompt-level rule and an architectural control can look identical until
something attacks them.

**Multi-turn and multi-agent settings.** These principles are drawn from single-agent, single-episode
work.

**Trained dispositions.** All of this concerns prompts, environments and scaffolds — what a given
setup can make a model do or prevent it from doing. None of it speaks to what the model is like.
